primary_citation: 47 C.F.R. §64.2010 (FCC CPNI Authentication Rules); implementing 47 U.S.C. §222 (Telecommunications Act of 1996, Pub. L. 104-104)
short_title: FCC CPNI Rules — Carrier Duty to Protect Customer Proprietary Network Information; AT&T SIM Swap Negligence Theory
one_line_rule: Telecommunications carriers must protect Customer Proprietary Network Information and use passwords/PINs (not biographical information alone) to authenticate account changes; failure to prevent fraudulent SIM swaps constitutes CPNI violation and supports negligence/UCL civil claims against the carrier.

att_liability_theory.no_private_right_of_action: 47 U.S.C. §222 does not create a private civil damages claim — civil liability runs through negligence and UCL
att_liability_theory.negligence_per_se: AT&T's violation of 47 C.F.R. §64.2010 authentication requirements = negligence per se; the regulatory standard defines the duty of care
att_liability_theory.actual_knowledge: AT&T paid $25M CPNI enforcement settlement in 2015 for authentication failures; AT&T had actual knowledge of SIM swap/authentication vulnerability when processing the fraudulent port
att_liability_theory.but_for_causation: AT&T is the but-for cause of all downstream harms — without AT&T's CPNI failure, no SIM swap, no interception, no account access, no financial fraud, no disability claim interference
att_liability_theory.joint_and_several: AT&T potentially jointly and severally liable with McClaran for all damages; the SIM swap attack required AT&T's negligent facilitation as an essential element
att_liability_theory.ucl_path: AT&T's CPNI violation = 'unlawful' business practice under UCL §17200; UCL adds injunction and restitution to negligence damages
att_liability_theory.fcc_complaint_track: Parallel FCC consumer complaint filing (fcc.gov/consumers/guides/filing-informal-complaint) triggers FCC enforcement investigation; regulatory track complements civil litigation
